item.title: We don’t want to silence our media, keep them talking – Rabuka
item.description: Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says the People’s Alliance is committed to media freedom and the free flow of information. Rabuka highlighted this during the PINA Summit in Savusavu while responding to questions from fijivillage News on whether the People’s Alliance will go into the elections with a clear message to guard media independence and freedom.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says the People’s Alliance is committed to media freedom and the free flow of information.

Rabuka highlighted this during the PINA Summit in Savusavu while responding to questions from fijivillage News on whether the People’s Alliance will go into the elections with a clear message to guard media independence and freedom.

The Prime Minister says the repeal of the media legislation was not for the Government, but for the people, to restore the free flow of communication between the people, the media and the rest of the world.

Rabuka says while the repeal appeared significant to the media, it was small compared with what happened in 1987.

He says about 10 years later, Her Majesty received him at the palace, but the authors of the media decree have not been able to speak to him face to face about it.

Rabuka says this shows the difference in their attitude towards what they do and what they bring into being.

The Prime Minister further says the Pacific should not silence its media because the free flow of information benefits the public, governments and news organisations.

He says open discussion is part of the Pacific way, adding that they talk and do not stop anybody from talking.

Rabuka says they do not want to silence the media and that the media should keep talking.

Asked about restrictions facing a newspaper in Samoa, Rabuka says Fiji’s experience showed that restricting the media was like operating in a dark house, as such restrictions deny people and governments information that benefits them both.

item.title: WATCH: Savusavu residents raise climate concerns directly with Kamikamica at FMA Town Hall
item.description: Savusavu residents got the chance to put their concerns directly to Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica when he attended the Fijian Media Association Public Town Hall Forum on climate change and environmental issues. The Pre-COP31 Climate Change Town Hall Forum was held at Nukubalavu Village in Savusavu.
item.content:encoded:
Savusavu residents got the chance to put their concerns directly to Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica when he attended the Fijian Media Association Public Town Hall Forum on climate change and environmental issues.

The Pre-COP31 Climate Change Town Hall Forum was held at Nukubalavu Village in Savusavu.

The forum, organised by the FMA , gave residents an opportunity to raise concerns about environmental and climate challenges affecting their communities, question Government action and propose practical solutions.

Kamikamica, joined by Minister for NDRMO Mosese Bulitavu, other Government officials and experts from regional agencies were in Savusavu for the PINA Media Summit.

The discussion was moderated by fijivillage News Director Vijay Narayan and Fiji Television Manager News Stella Taoi.

Residents shared their own experiences, including changes they have observed, challenges affecting their livelihoods and solutions they believe should receive greater attention.

Questions around Government responses and the support needed by communities also formed part of the discussion.

The forum was livestreamed across participating media platforms, including fijivillage.

It was held alongside the 8th Pacific Media Summit, hosted by the Fijian Media Association and the Pacific Islands News Association.

The town hall is aimed at bringing community voices into the regional gathering of Pacific journalists and media leaders, while creating a direct platform for public discussion and accountability on climate and environmental issues.

The event is supported by PACMAS and forms part of the Fijian Media Association’s collaborative town hall initiative involving Fiji’s media organisations.

item.title: WOWS Kids co-founders recall daughter Tae seeing death not as failure but victory
item.description: Knowing her cancer was terminal, the eldest daughter of WOWS Kids co-founders Sina and Taholo Kami faced the final chapter of her life with a remarkable acceptance of death, telling her parents that dying would not be a failure but a victory. item.content:encoded:
Knowing her cancer was terminal, the eldest daughter of WOWS Kids co-founders Sina and Taholo Kami faced the final chapter of her life with a remarkable acceptance of death, telling her parents that dying would not be a failure but a victory.

Speaking on Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan, Tae’s mother, Sina Kami, recalls her daughter asking whether she would be okay when Tae died, sharing a question no parent would want to face but one that became part of the family’s journey of faith, love and acceptance.

Sina says she assured Tae that when God was ready to take her home, she would be okay because she believed God would take care of her daughter.

Insert:Taholo Kami shares how his daughter spoke about her own death 23rd Sept

Sina says Tae loved playing the guitar, reading and spending time with her sisters and friends, while one of her favourite songs was His Eye Is on the Sparrow.

She says Tae also prayed regularly, sometimes quietly and sometimes out loud, and would pray for people who came to visit her.

Tae also kept journals, which her father Taholo says documented the struggles she faced as a young teenager, including the difficulty of looking in the mirror as cancer affected her face.

Despite those struggles, Sina says Tae told students at Queensland College that although cancer had affected her face, her faith remained strong.

Taholo says Tae also found an outlet through music and began writing Walk On, Walk Strong after the family moved into their home.

He says Tae had written the first verse and chorus and would play the song for visitors, including musicians such as Randy Thaman and Gonai.

However, in January or February 2008, the family learned that Tae’s cancer was terminal after she developed a cough and scans revealed spots in her lungs.

Taholo says Tae cried on the way home from the clinic but later returned with plans for her funeral.

He says Tae asked her parents to finish the song with her, and together they wrote the second verse, reflecting her belief that death was not a failure but a victory.

He says Tae later told a Tongan musician that she believed God would create a ministry from her pain and that she accepted 15 years as the life God had given her.

item.title: Sigatoka couple turns family garage operation into growing export business
item.description: 31-year-old Vinesh Varun Sharma and his wife Vandhana started Vinesh Export in 2023, initially converting their garage into a makeshift packhouse as they worked to get the business off the ground. The couple now source fruits, vegetables and root crops from farmers in Sigatoka, other parts of the Western Division and Central Viti Levu.
item.content:encoded:
31-year-old Vinesh Varun Sharma and his wife Vandhana started Vinesh Export in 2023, initially converting their garage into a makeshift packhouse as they worked to get the business off the ground.

The couple now source fruits, vegetables and root crops from farmers in Sigatoka, other parts of the Western Division and Central Viti Levu.

Produce including eggplant, pawpaw, okra, chillies, ginger, cassava and dalo is exported to New Zealand, while pearl guava is sent to Japan.

Sharma says the business exported 43,560 kilograms of produce in 2024, earning $348,480.

A year later, exports had increased to 81,100 kilograms, with income rising to $648,800.

Sharma says the money earned is reinvested into the business to help it continue growing.

The business is also providing another market for local farmers, collecting vegetables from them every Thursday and Saturday for export.

As the operation expanded, Vinesh Export received support through the Ministry of Agriculture's Commercial Agriculture Development Programme, which provided a packhouse and cooler valued at $87,398.

The facilities have allowed the family to handle larger volumes of produce while maintaining the quality required for export.

Vinesh Export currently employs five full-time and 10 casual workers.

However, expanding the business has also brought challenges.

The company currently has one three-tonne truck to transport produce to the airport and sometimes has to make two trips when export orders are high.

Sharma says maintaining the quality of produce is another important part of the operation, as products that do not meet export standards cannot be sent overseas.

Despite these challenges, the family plans to continue expanding the business and creating more opportunities for farmers to supply produce for overseas markets.

For Sharma and Vandhana, the business has come a long way from the makeshift packhouse in their family garage, and they are now focused on expanding the operation further.
